[*]Act 3 is considered to be the ending to the game, but it's completely unsatisfying and sudden, which makes you want to continue and finish Act 4 for the "true ending." Speaking of which...
[*]ACT 4 CAN GO DIE IN THE HOTTEST FIRES OF MOUNT DOOM
[/list]

This game feels like a fortress siege simulator that someone tacked a story onto at the last second. While capturing a fortress is fun and requires a lot of thoughtful setup and strategy, defending those fortresses (which is pretty much the entirety of Act 4) is not nearly as fun, as you basically just juggle one captain fight after another while your defending captains bleed out at a distance because they're very incompetent unless they're a Slayer, Assassin, or Tank class. If they'd put as much work into making Defense missions as dynamic and cinematic as Attack missions, they would have been much more fun. This is a shame, because you spend more time defending than attacking.

Many have complained about the lootbox system, but I disagree with the assertion that you need them. Yes the idea of lootboxes is dumb and yes too many games utilize it nowadays, but I literally used 3 of the orcs that I drew from them, and they still weren't as powerful as the orcs I got by just playing the game. You absolutely do not need the lootboxes to beat this game, contrary to what some say (and I beat it on the highest difficulty, so I know what I'm talking about). The thing you really need to do in order to keep your orcs strong is remember to level up Talion, because your orc followers cannot exceed his level. Just be sure to equip the white runes to your armor and cloak, and you'll level up quickly enough. I reached the max level, 60, before completing Act 4, and I never used a Lootbox XP boost or any other bonuses besides the runes.

And finally, my thoughts on Act 4... This final part of the game single-handedly makes me want to change my review to "Not Recommended." Acts 1-3 are very story driven and focus on development of Talion and Celebrimbor as they use their new ring of power to turn Sauron's armies against him, and after a climactic conclusion to Act 3 (which had a twist that EVERYBODY saw coming), the game devolves into a grind-fest of nothing but fortress defense missions. THAT'S IT. THAT'S THE BOWTIE THEY PUT ON THIS PUPPY. YOU HAVE TO DEFEND YOUR FORTRESSES 20 BLEEPING TIMES IN ORDER TO GET THE "TRUE ENDING." But the problem is, you captured the previous fortresses with lower leveled orcs, and now the new orcs attacking you out-level them by at least 15 levels, so now you have to grind XP for all your orcs one at a time before you even begin to tackle all those defense missions. I absolutely hate this part of the game, because it took everything that was fun about playing it (dominating orcs, building your army's strength, and adding upgrades to your fortress) and made it a chore. I was ready to blow my brains out from boredom by the time I finally leveled up my last orc and was ready for the final bout of assaults.

Why do I recommend it after all this? Because it gave me so much satisfaction just by playing it. After all the bullshit, after all the hard work, after all the grinding defense missions, it felt SO GOOD to sit back and watch the final cinematic. This game reminded me of Dark Souls, because it focuses on creating a sense of accomplishment after a difficult challenge. The randomly generated encounters kept it fresh, and in the end, I found it easy to truly immerse myself. Overall, I had fun, even if that fun evolved from tactile fun to the relief of accomplishment. Whenever I dominated an entire pack of Caragors with one move and turned them on their handlers, when one of my orcs leveled himself up only to turn to me and say "Don't tell me you didn't see this coming?" as he drew his morgul blade and sicked 3 Captains on me in an elaborate ambush/betrayal, when I pitted two orcs who were blood-brothers against each other and watched them become conflicted about it, when I threw the head of an enemy Warlord off a tower after capturing the fortress, when I caused a Captain who should've killed me to flee in terror because he was afraid of spiders, when I rode a Graug and ENGAGED IN AN EFFING FIERY FISTFIGHT WITH AN ARMORED BALROG... it all reminded me why I kept playing this game. Behind all the frustration, pointless grinding, and stupid AI, this game is actually fun to play, pure and simple.

I can only recommend getting this game if it's on sale for $25-$30 or so. I don't think it's worth more than that, but if you love sandbox games or loved Shadow of Mordor, then you might get a kick out of this one. Just be warned of the frustrations you will have to endure before the game ends.

[b][u]HINT[/u]: I found a quick way to level your orcs... Most orcs from the Trickster class will tend to retreat once their health gets halfway depleted. Find a Trickster orc of a very high level (higher than 60 is ideal), and send your lowly leveled orcs to kill/ambush them. Then, help them out in that mission by fighting the Trickster orc yourself, and when he starts to retreat, let him escape. Your orc will get the victory and up to a 20 level boost, and that Trickster orc will still be alive to use the same trick on again. Rinse and repeat this for all the rest of your orcs until they're sitting pretty at levels of 55-60.
You're Welcome![/b]
Shadow of Mordor objectively has the better story, this game has the better loop/grind.

I'm what you'd call a Lord of the Rings fan. 

You've probably heard by now the writers have taken some liberties with Tolkien's world. Some would even call these divergences sacrilege and, by and large, I'd tend to agree. Most of the new characters, reveals, twists, and retellings could be forgiven if they were any good. Unfortunately, they're forgettable and tropey, silly and trite more often than not. That doesn't mean you should pass on this game. 

The stories that are the most fun are the ones you make for yourself, and that is where this game excels. The oft mentioned Nemesis system is brilliant and improved upon significantly past its predecessor. My recommendation would be to pump up the difficultly and allow yourself to die. That's right. Don't coast through the combat, or it will begin to feel repetitive and thoughtless. Instead, give yourself a challenge, think about the enemy encounters, and allow them to beat you - because when they do, they'll remember it. Next time you swing by their neck of the woods, a story will begin to emerge and, unlike the scripted encounters, you'll actually care this time. Everyone you fight has a name and rank, special abilities, weaknesses, fears, and strengths. That orc who hates fire will definitely remember when you tried to burn him to death. That commander you killed came back from the dead, but now he's out of his mind and talking to ghosts. These are the stories you'll care about after 50 or 100 or 500 hours. 

Graphically, this game comes in below most other AAA experiences, even on Max settings with a high framerate. With that said, the orc designs are stunning and imaginative. Particle effects and combat animations don't get old too quickly. Most environment designs are forgettable until you unlock the Siege portion of the game several hours in. These all-out war, ride of the Rohirrim, Battle of Helm's Deep-style battles have you conquering various strongholds which end in a climactic mini-boss fight. Tackling these on harder difficulties is a rush and require careful consideration.

All in all, I enjoyed my time with the game. It started to grind toward a halt in the final a few hours, but by then I'd already had my fun. I would not recommend purchasing this game at full price, but if you can get the Definitive Edition on sale it's worth every penny, regardless of it's mediocre storytelling. If you're here because you're a LotR fan, tread with caution. This game will disrespect you. If you want an open world action game where you can craft stories for yourself, then slip on your ring of power and do your best to ignore all that Shelob nonsense.

Cheers!

[b]UPDATE:
WB and Monolith have removed pay to win elements from this game, including lootboxes. I shall keep this review negative however, as a lesson to Publishers and Devs alike that this kind of behavior will not be tolerated.[/b]


[h1]Tl'dr version: [/h1]

[b]An amazing improvement upon the original, completely contaminated by some of the worst industry practices we have yet seen. Make no mistake, if the consumer base does not stop this now, we will be seeing not only microtransactions in $60 games but further degradation of the base game for them to wring every last ounce of money from us. DO NOT BUY THE LOOTBOXES.[/b]

You can follow me, and see the rest of my work here:
http://steamcommunity.com/id/StarSide/myworkshopfiles/?section=guides

[h1]Elaborated version:[/h1]

Maybe from that you can already tell I will not just be talking about the base-game of Shadow of War for the whole review. Most reviewers policy is to separate industry practices from the game to judge the game "on its own merits". Well, here's my issues with that. If you are compromising the product on purpose, in order to drag the game out, or purposely tear the game apart in order for you sell us content later down the line, that is most definitely an already compromised (ethically and mechanically) product. 

If WB had kept their grubby mitts of this game, I would most definitely have given this a positive review. However, since that is not what they have done, this review will remain negative. 

[b]Microtransactions.[/b]

Some in-depth analysis here. Firstly, the infamous loot box situation. You can buy orks from loots boxes, not just getting them out in the in-game world. This completely breaks in-game immersion and the economy of the game. You can either choose to ignore the loot boxes and go at it vanilla, where you're missing out on possible high-level minions, as the game was obviously intended, as the level of orks you find are introduced on a gradient; the higher level you are, the better orks you will find. Additionally, what are essentially ads for the lootboxes keep popping up in game, where you are prompted to go and buy them. Also, if you want any hope of being 'competitive' in the online game mode Shadow Wars, you'll need some super powerful orks, something the lootboxes have the slight possibility to help with. 

Consequently, you will notice every dynamic in the game becomes centered around these things in some form of another:

You want an high level ork? Cough up! 
You want to upgrade your weapons and armor? You'll need additional gems to do that, cough up!
You want to play multiplayer? Better have some good orks, so cough up!!

Whether the game would have been constructed like this without the cancer that is WarnerBrothers getting their claws into the mechanics of the game is completely moot. 

Now, with that out of the way, let's talk about the game.

[b]Story.[/b]

You a lord of the rings lore fan? This is going to be a rough ride. 
The game, for better or for worse, plays fast and lose with the canon to such an extent you wonder why not just set this in the time of the silmerilian and call it a day. However, if you can get past the desecration of established law (which I can), the story is actually quite compelling. 

Following on the last game, Ranger Talion and his ancient dead elf-friendo Calimbrimbor have made a new ring of power, just like Saurons. Great! What could go wrong. Turns out quite a lot actually. What follows is an epic, continent spanning war between the 'Bright Lord' and Sauron. All sorts of shenanigans ensue! Just don't get too disappointed if you were expecting high-brow Shakespeare. 


[b]Movement and Combat.[/b]

Like Shadows of Mordor but better. Everything is back from the last game, but with added upppf. Movement is buttery smooth, and really the game plays just like every other third-person openworld, Arkyum style game. Speaking of which, the combat system is straight outta Batman, which isn't a bad thing. 
Combat is fun and Talion's wraith powers are suitably beefed up from the last game. 

[b]The Nemesis system.[/b]
I was going to add this to the last section however, it more or less is one of the most original ideas in the last decade in gaming. Essentially, the Nemesis system allows every individual ork to remember you, and everything you've done to them. Burn that ork captain in a fire, he might come for you later on. This is extended to the 'meta game' aspect for creating armies. Your generals might betray you, or save your life. This creates some of the best dynamic stories in gaming really. However, sometimes the betrayals get a little too common, and you'll find yourself trying to game the system in order to keep your orks on your side. 
I won't say anything more, it really is something better to experience for yourself. 

[b]Sound.[/b]
Not the best, not the worst. Voice acting is passable, with a few exceptions. Talion seems mostly asleep during his cutscenes, the voice actor is clearly phoning it in for his paycheck at this point. On the other hand, Calimbrimbor is the star of the show. His gravely tones are both charismatic and slightly scary, especially when he gets all shouty. 
Combat noises are also quite good. Swords ring and the screams of orks will pervade your ears constantly. In this universe, all orks seem to have a slightly comical British cocny accent. You'll either love it or hate it. 


[b]Conclusion[/b]
Not concentrating on the poor industry behavior, this is a great game. However, I will not simply segregate them out of the review, because this stuff definitely effects the end product. Great game! But make a statement and wait for this to get to a low price. And DON'T, DON'T, DON'T buy those damn lootboxes!!
